subtopic_detail: Adolescent unable to initiate sleep before the early hours who sleeps normally when free of a school schedule
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 16 year old boy brought in by his mother because he cannot get up for school and has missed twelve days this term. He says he lies awake until about three in the morning however early he goes to bed, then cannot be woken at seven.

On school holidays he falls asleep at about three and wakes around eleven, sleeps straight through, and describes himself as fine and full of energy. He denies feeling flat or hopeless, still plays basketball twice a week, sees his friends, and is not worried about school or being bullied. He drinks no coffee or energy drinks and uses no substances.

data_table.Examination: Alert and engaged with normal affect and reactive mood, no psychomotor slowing, body mass index 21 kg/m2, no goitre, tonsils not enlarged, no snoring reported by the family
data_table.Investigations: Sleep diary over two weeks confirms sleep onset between 2.30 and 3.30 am with a spontaneous wake time of 11 am when unconstrained, full blood count, iron studies and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a short course of temazepam to be taken at his intended bedtime
options.rationale: A hypnotic forces sleep onset without moving the underlying circadian timing, so the wake time stays late and the sleepiness continues, and benzodiazepines are not recommended for adolescents given tolerance and dependence. The problem is the phase of the clock rather than an inability to sleep. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation Australia: Delayed sleep wake phase disorder)
source_refs: Sleep Health Foundation Australia: Delayed sleep wake phase disorder

options.text: Commence sertraline and arrange psychological review for underlying depression
options.rationale: Depression in adolescents frequently presents with sleep disturbance and school refusal, which makes it the correct alternative to consider here. It is argued against by preserved energy, continued sport and friendships, an absence of low mood or anhedonia, and by sleep that is entirely normal in quality and duration once the schedule allows it. (Source: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Advise low dose melatonin several hours before sleep with morning bright light
options.rationale: Melatonin taken in the early evening, well before the intended sleep time, acts chronobiologically to advance the circadian phase rather than as a sedative, and bright light on waking anchors the advance by suppressing the endogenous melatonin tail. Combining the two with a gradual advance of the sleep schedule is the evidence based treatment for a delayed circadian phase in adolescents. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation Australia: Delayed sleep wake phase disorder)
source_refs: Sleep Health Foundation Australia: Delayed sleep wake phase disorder

options.text: Refer for overnight polysomnography before beginning any specific treatment
options.rationale: Polysomnography is indicated when obstructive sleep apnoea, periodic limb movements or narcolepsy is suspected, signalled by snoring, witnessed apnoeas, cataplexy or sleep that is unrefreshing despite adequate duration. A two week sleep diary has already established the diagnosis, and a laboratory study adds cost and delay. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation Australia: Delayed sleep wake phase disorder)
source_refs: Sleep Health Foundation Australia: Delayed sleep wake phase disorder

options.text: Advise removing devices from the bedroom as the sole intervention for now
options.rationale: Reducing evening light exposure from screens is a necessary component of treatment because light after dusk delays the circadian phase further, and it should certainly be advised. Used alone it rarely shifts an established delay of several hours, and the timed melatonin and morning light that actively move the phase are what produce the change. (Source: Sleep Health Foundation Australia: Delayed sleep wake phase disorder)
source_refs: Sleep Health Foundation Australia: Delayed sleep wake phase disorder

explanation.summary: Delayed sleep wake phase disorder is the commonest circadian rhythm disorder of adolescence, affecting up to around one in ten teenagers, and arises from a physiological pubertal delay in melatonin onset compounded by evening light exposure and social scheduling. The diagnostic signature is that sleep itself is entirely normal in latency, quality and duration once the person is allowed to sleep at their preferred times, which is why the holiday pattern is the most useful question in the history. It is separated from insomnia, where sleep is poor regardless of timing, and from depression, where mood, energy and interest are affected independently of the sleep schedule. Treatment combines a gradual advance of the sleep schedule, low dose melatonin timed several hours before the desired sleep onset for its phase shifting rather than sedative effect, morning bright light, and strict evening light restriction. Melatonin use in adolescents for this indication is outside the registered indication in Australia and is prescribed with that explained to the family.
key_points: Normal sleep on holidays with an unconstrained schedule is the diagnostic clue
The disorder is one of timing rather than of sleep quality or quantity
Melatonin is given several hours before the intended sleep time for phase shifting
Morning bright light is required to anchor the advance and prevent drift back
Hypnotics move sleep onset without moving the wake time and are not indicated
explanation.pearls: Dose the melatonin by timing rather than by amount: 0.5 to 1 mg taken about five hours before current sleep onset produces a larger phase advance than a much bigger dose taken at bedtime, where it acts only as a mild sedative and leaves the circadian delay untouched.

sources.label: Sleep Health Foundation Australia: Delayed sleep wake phase disorder
RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Repetitive hair pulling with relief afterwards and broken hairs of varying length without scalp inflammation
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 19 year old university student who has two bald patches at the crown of her scalp. She tells you she pulls her hair out, mostly while studying at night or watching television, and that she feels a building tension beforehand and a sense of relief once she has pulled.

She has been doing this for about three years, has tried wearing a beanie and cutting her nails short, and is embarrassed enough that she has stopped going to the gym. She is not distressed by thoughts of contamination or harm, does not check or count, and has no rituals she feels compelled to perform. She swallows no hair and has no abdominal pain.

data_table.Examination: Two irregular patches of hair loss at the crown containing broken hairs of varying lengths, scalp skin normal with no scaling, erythema, pustules or scarring, no exclamation mark hairs, eyebrows and eyelashes intact, no abdominal mass
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies and thyroid function all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Refer for habit reversal training with an appropriately trained therapist
options.rationale: Habit reversal training teaches awareness of the antecedent urge and situations, and substitutes a competing response that is incompatible with pulling, and it has the strongest evidence of any treatment for this condition. Behavioural therapy outperforms medication in trials and is recommended as first line in a young person who is motivated and already attempting self management. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor at a dose used for compulsions
options.rationale: High dose serotonergic treatment is first line for obsessive compulsive disorder, where obsessions drive compulsions performed to reduce anxiety. Hair pulling is a body focused repetitive behaviour driven by tension and relief without obsessional content, and randomised evidence for serotonin reuptake inhibitors in this condition is weak. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Prescribe topical minoxidil solution to the affected areas of the scalp
options.rationale: Minoxidil promotes regrowth in androgenetic alopecia, where follicles miniaturise progressively rather than being mechanically extracted. Regrowth here occurs once pulling stops, so a topical agent treats the visible consequence while the behaviour continues. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology

options.text: Commence oral N acetylcysteine and review the response after three months
options.rationale: N acetylcysteine has shown benefit in adults in small randomised trials and is a reasonable adjunct or option when behavioural therapy is unavailable or has failed. It is not the first line treatment, and the evidence in adolescents and young adults has been less consistent than in older adults. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Commence a low dose antipsychotic to augment behavioural strategies she has tried
options.rationale: Antipsychotic augmentation is used in treatment resistant obsessive compulsive disorder after adequate serotonergic and behavioural treatment has failed, and olanzapine has limited supporting data in hair pulling. Starting it before any structured behavioural therapy accepts metabolic and movement risk for an unproven gain. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

explanation.summary: Trichotillomania is classified with the obsessive compulsive and related disorders but behaves differently in treatment, since it is a body focused repetitive behaviour driven by mounting tension and subsequent relief rather than by intrusive obsessions. It has a lifetime prevalence of one to two per cent, typically begins in early adolescence, and affects women far more often in clinical samples. The clinical signs are irregular patches containing hairs broken at different lengths with entirely normal underlying skin, which separate it from alopecia areata with its smooth patches and exclamation mark hairs, and from tinea capitis with its scaling and inflammation. Habit reversal training is the first line treatment and remains the only intervention with consistent randomised support, delivered alone or within a broader behavioural framework. N acetylcysteine is a reasonable pharmacological option in adults, and any child or adult who eats the pulled hair needs assessment for a trichobezoar, which can obstruct or perforate.
key_points: Tension before pulling with relief afterwards distinguishes it from obsessive compulsive disorder
Broken hairs of differing lengths with normal scalp skin is the examination signature
Habit reversal training is first line and outperforms medication
N acetylcysteine has modest randomised support in adults as an alternative
Ask about eating the hair, which risks a trichobezoar needing surgery
explanation.pearls: Ask directly whether she swallows the hair she pulls: trichophagia occurs in roughly one in five people with this condition and a trichobezoar can extend from the stomach into the small bowel, presenting with an epigastric mass and obstruction that requires surgical removal.

sources.label: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

subtopic_detail: Accumulation of possessions with distress at discarding and unusable living space in a late middle aged adult
stem:
You are the general practitioner asked to see a 58 year old woman after her daughter contacted the practice. On a home visit you find narrow walkways between stacked newspapers, boxes and shopping bags, the kitchen bench unusable and the bath full of stored items.

She tells you each item might be needed one day and becomes visibly distressed and tearful when her daughter suggests removing anything. She does not describe intrusive thoughts about contamination or harm, performs no washing, checking or counting rituals, and says she simply cannot bear to waste things. She is oriented, manages her own finances and medication accurately, and shops for herself. She has no delusional beliefs about the items and knows the state of the house is a problem.

data_table.Examination: Well groomed, normal affect with appropriate reactivity, no psychomotor change, no evidence of psychosis, clock drawing test normal
data_table.Investigations: Montreal Cognitive Assessment 28 out of 30, full blood count, urea creatinine and electrolytes, thyroid function and vitamin B12 all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence a high dose serotonin reuptake inhibitor as used for compulsions
options.rationale: High dose serotonergic treatment is the pharmacological backbone of obsessive compulsive disorder, where compulsions are performed to neutralise intrusive obsessions. Hoarding disorder responds considerably less well to these agents in trials and lacks the obsessional structure, which is why it was separated as its own diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Arrange a council clean out of the property while she stays with her daughter
options.rationale: Forced clearance removes the immediate fire and public health hazard and is occasionally unavoidable under environmental health legislation. Done without the person's engagement it is experienced as traumatic, damages the therapeutic relationship, and the accumulation typically returns within a year because the underlying beliefs about possessions are untouched. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Refer for a capacity assessment with a view to guardianship for her affairs
options.rationale: Guardianship applies when a person lacks decision making capacity because of impairment, and her cognitive testing is normal and she manages finances and medication accurately. Making an unwise or harmful choice is not itself evidence of incapacity. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy developed specifically for hoarding
options.rationale: The treatment with the best evidence is a hoarding specific cognitive behavioural protocol covering motivational work, training in decision making and categorisation, graded practice at discarding and reduction of acquiring, usually with home based sessions. It is distinct from standard obsessive compulsive protocols, which perform poorly in this population, and engagement is the central therapeutic task given typically limited motivation. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Commence a low dose antipsychotic to reduce her attachment to the possessions
options.rationale: Antipsychotic treatment would be appropriate if the accumulation were driven by delusional beliefs, for example that the items are needed for a mission or are being sent by someone. She retains insight that the state of the house is a problem, which places the beliefs about possessions on an overvalued rather than delusional spectrum. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

explanation.summary: Hoarding disorder was separated from obsessive compulsive disorder because it differs in phenomenology, course and treatment response, and it affects around two per cent of adults with a prevalence rising with age. The core features are persistent difficulty discarding possessions regardless of value, distress at the prospect of discarding, and accumulation that renders living areas unusable for their intended purpose. Insight varies widely and referrals are often generated by family, neighbours or environmental health rather than by the person, which makes motivational engagement the first therapeutic task. The differential includes obsessive compulsive disorder with hoarding driven by contamination fears, psychotic disorders with delusional accumulation, frontotemporal dementia where hoarding appears alongside behavioural change and executive decline, and severe depression where the accumulation reflects inactivity. Hoarding specific cognitive behavioural therapy is the treatment of choice, medication has a limited role, and the immediate practical priority is managing fire risk, falls risk and access for emergency services.
key_points: Difficulty discarding, distress on discarding and unusable living space define the disorder
It responds poorly to standard obsessive compulsive protocols and to serotonergic medication
Hoarding specific cognitive behavioural therapy with home sessions is first line
Forced clearance without engagement is traumatic and accumulation usually recurs
New onset hoarding with behavioural change warrants assessment for frontotemporal dementia
explanation.pearls: Assess fire risk at the first visit and notify the fire service where local arrangements allow: blocked exits and stacked combustible material mean deaths in house fires are many times more likely in hoarded properties, and that risk cannot wait for the months that therapy takes to work.

sources.label: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

subtopic_detail: Severe irritability and low mood confined to the week before menstruation with prospective rating over two cycles
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 33 year old woman who says she becomes a different person for about a week each month. She describes irritability that has frightened her children, tearfulness, a sense of being overwhelmed and food cravings, and says it lifts within a day or two of her period starting and she then feels completely well.

This has gone on for two years and has worsened since the birth of her second child. She has kept daily symptom ratings for the past two cycles at your request, and they show scores in the normal range throughout the first half of each cycle. She is using condoms for contraception and does not wish to start hormonal contraception. She has no history of depression outside this pattern and no thoughts of self harm.

data_table.Examination: Normal affect at today's visit on day 6 of her cycle, no psychomotor change, body mass index 26 kg/m2, no goitre
data_table.Investigations: Prospective daily symptom ratings over two consecutive cycles show a greater than 50 per cent rise in scores in the luteal phase with full remission by day 4, thyroid function and full blood count within normal limits

options.text: Commence a combined oral contraceptive containing drospirenone continuously
options.rationale: A drospirenone containing combined pill taken with a shortened or omitted hormone free interval has randomised evidence in this condition and is a reasonable first line option for many women. She has specifically declined hormonal contraception, which removes it as the recommendation she would accept. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal and women's mental health guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal and women's mental health guidance

options.text: Commence a serotonin reuptake inhibitor taken from ovulation until menstruation
options.rationale: Serotonergic antidepressants work within one to two days in this condition rather than over the weeks required in major depression, which is why intermittent dosing restricted to the luteal phase is as effective as continuous treatment and halves total drug exposure and adverse effects. Sertraline, escitalopram and fluoxetine all have randomised support for this pattern of use. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal and women's mental health guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal and women's mental health guidance

options.text: Commence a serotonin reuptake inhibitor taken continuously every day of the cycle
options.rationale: Continuous dosing is equally effective and is preferred when the woman also has a depressive or anxiety disorder outside the luteal phase, or when cycles are irregular and the luteal phase cannot be predicted. With clean prospective ratings showing full remission in the follicular phase, daily dosing means two extra weeks of exposure each month for no additional benefit. (Source: RANZCP: Perinatal and women's mental health guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Perinatal and women's mental health guidance

options.text: Recommend a calcium supplement with regular aerobic exercise for three cycles
options.rationale: Calcium supplementation and exercise have modest supporting evidence and are worth recommending alongside other treatment for milder premenstrual symptoms. Symptoms severe enough to affect her relationship with her children warrant a treatment with a substantial effect size as the primary recommendation. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders

options.text: Refer for a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist with add back hormone therapy
options.rationale: Ovarian suppression with an agonist is highly effective and is used to confirm that symptoms are ovulation dependent before considering definitive surgery. It causes a hypo oestrogenic state with bone loss, so it is a specialist option reserved for severe symptoms that have failed serotonergic and hormonal treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Premenstrual disorders

explanation.summary: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder affects around three to eight per cent of women of reproductive age and is defined by affective and physical symptoms confined to the luteal phase with full remission shortly after menstruation begins. Diagnosis requires prospective daily ratings over at least two cycles, because retrospective report matches prospective data poorly and around half of women who report the pattern turn out to have a continuous mood or anxiety disorder with premenstrual worsening instead. That distinction changes treatment entirely, since premenstrual exacerbation of an underlying disorder requires continuous treatment of that disorder. The condition reflects abnormal central sensitivity to normal fluctuations in progesterone metabolites rather than abnormal hormone levels, so measuring hormones is unhelpful. First line treatment is a serotonergic antidepressant given continuously or restricted to the luteal phase, or a combined oral contraceptive containing drospirenone with a shortened hormone free interval, and severe refractory cases may be offered ovarian suppression or, rarely, bilateral oophorectomy.
key_points: Prospective daily ratings over two cycles are required to make the diagnosis
Full remission in the follicular phase separates it from premenstrual exacerbation
Hormone levels are normal and measuring them does not assist
Serotonergic antidepressants act within one to two days in this condition
Luteal phase dosing matches continuous dosing in efficacy with half the exposure
explanation.pearls: Check that the follicular phase ratings are genuinely normal before choosing intermittent dosing: any residual symptoms in the first half of the cycle mean the diagnosis is premenstrual exacerbation of an underlying mood or anxiety disorder, and luteal dosing will then fail because the baseline condition goes untreated.

subtopic_detail: Third relapse of psychosis each following cessation of oral medication with full response while taking it
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 27 year old man on the ward two weeks into his third admission in two years. Each admission has followed him stopping his tablets, and on each occasion his symptoms have fully resolved within three to four weeks of restarting the same medication.

He is now settled, no longer describes voices, and can discuss his illness openly. He tells you the tablets do help but that he forgets them once he is feeling well and finds taking something every day a daily reminder that he is unwell. He uses no alcohol or other drugs, and urine drug screens on each admission have been negative. He has had no movement side effects and his weight has been stable.

data_table.Examination: Calm, cooperative, no thought disorder, no perceptual disturbance elicited, partial insight with agreement that medication has helped, no rigidity, tremor or abnormal involuntary movements
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea creatinine and electrolytes, liver function, fasting lipids and glucose all within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management on discharge?

options.text: Switch to clozapine given that he has now relapsed on three separate occasions
options.rationale: Clozapine is indicated for treatment resistant illness, defined as failure of two adequate trials of different antipsychotics at adequate dose and duration. His illness has responded fully every time he has taken medication, so these are relapses from non adherence rather than treatment resistance, and clozapine would bring haematological and metabolic monitoring burdens without addressing the actual problem. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Increase the oral dose and arrange weekly community follow up after discharge
options.rationale: Dose escalation is the response to an inadequate symptomatic response at an adequate dose, which is not the situation when symptoms resolve reliably on the current dose. Raising the dose increases side effect burden and gives him one more reason to stop taking it. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Add a mood stabiliser to reduce the frequency of further relapses of illness
options.rationale: Adjunctive mood stabilisers are used where there is a significant affective component, for schizoaffective presentations, or for persistent aggression, none of which is described here. Adding a second daily medication compounds the very burden he identifies as the reason he stops. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Apply for a community treatment order to enforce ongoing oral medication
options.rationale: A compulsory order requires that the criteria under the relevant state mental health legislation are met and that less restrictive options have been considered, and it is not a substitute for a treatment he is willing to accept. He is engaged, agrees the medication helps and is participating in planning, so a voluntary arrangement should be offered first. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Offer transfer to a long acting injectable form of his current antipsychotic
options.rationale: A depot preparation removes the daily decision that he identifies as the point of failure, maintains plasma levels for weeks and makes disengagement visible to the team immediately rather than after symptoms return. Australian guidance recommends offering a long acting injectable early in the course of illness, particularly after relapse attributable to non adherence, rather than reserving it for repeated failure. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Relapse in schizophrenia is dominated by non adherence, which carries roughly a fivefold increase in relapse risk, and each psychotic episode is associated with incremental loss of function and a longer time to remission. Distinguishing non adherence from treatment resistance is therefore the central question when someone relapses repeatedly, and the discriminator is whether symptoms remit when the medication is actually taken. Long acting injectable antipsychotics reduce relapse and rehospitalisation compared with oral equivalents in cohort and mirror image studies, and Australian guidance recommends offering them early rather than after multiple failures, including after a first episode. The historical reluctance to offer depot treatment to younger people with good insight is not supported by evidence and reflects clinician rather than patient preference, since many people prefer not to take a daily tablet. Choice of agent is guided by response to a prior oral trial of the same molecule, and oral supplementation is given during the loading period for agents that take weeks to reach steady state.
key_points: Full remission whenever medication is taken indicates non adherence, not resistance
Clozapine requires two adequate trials of different antipsychotics to have failed
Long acting injectables reduce relapse and rehospitalisation versus oral equivalents
Australian guidance supports offering depot early, including after a first episode
Non adherence becomes immediately visible with a depot rather than weeks later
explanation.pearls: Choose the injectable form of the oral drug he has already responded to and tolerated, and continue oral cover during the loading phase: agents such as paliperidone palmitate reach therapeutic levels quickly with a loading regimen, whereas others take six to eight weeks, and a relapse during that window is almost always a loading error rather than a treatment failure.

sources.label: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Early prescription requests and multiple prescribers on long term opioid therapy for non cancer back pain
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 54 year old man who has taken modified release oxycodone for six years for back pain following a work injury. He has asked for his script eight days early on three occasions this year, saying the pain has been worse.

The real time prescription monitoring system shows he has also received oxycodone from two other practices in the past four months. He has stopped attending the gym programme he was doing, sleeps poorly, and says the tablets take the edge off but no longer help as they once did. He does not inject, uses no heroin or stimulants, drinks two beers most evenings, and has never had an overdose.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72 per minute, blood pressure 132/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: No pinpoint pupils, no sedation, no track marks, lumbar movement restricted by pain with negative straight leg raise, power reflexes and sensation in both legs within normal limits, no saddle anaesthesia
data_table.Investigations: Current daily dose equivalent to 80 mg of oral morphine, liver function and renal function within normal limits, urine drug screen positive for oxycodone only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Stop the oxycodone immediately and prescribe oral naltrexone to prevent relapse
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation after six years of continuous use precipitates withdrawal, drives people to obtain opioids elsewhere, and is associated with increased overdose death and suicide in cohort studies. Naltrexone requires a completed withdrawal before it can be started safely at all. (Source: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice)
source_refs: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice

options.text: Continue the current dose and add pregabalin for a neuropathic component
options.rationale: Pregabalin is used for confirmed neuropathic pain, which is argued against here by a negative straight leg raise with normal power, reflexes and sensation. Combining a gabapentinoid with an opioid also substantially increases the risk of respiratory depression and overdose death. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Analgesic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Analgesic

options.text: Establish a single prescriber agreement and begin a gradual dose reduction
options.rationale: Consolidating prescribing to one practitioner and one pharmacy stops the multiple sourcing that the monitoring system has identified, and a slow reduction of the order of ten per cent every two to four weeks is tolerable and avoids precipitating withdrawal. Reduction is indicated because the opioid has lost effect, function is deteriorating and the behaviour signals loss of control, and it is combined with active non opioid pain management. (Source: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice)
source_refs: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice

options.text: Increase to transdermal fentanyl to provide more stable analgesic blood levels
options.rationale: Rotating to a more potent lipophilic opioid at a time of escalating use and declining function raises the total opioid load and the overdose risk, and conversion errors between oxycodone and fentanyl are a recognised cause of death. Steadier blood levels do not address tolerance or the loss of control. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Opioid analgesics)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Opioid analgesics

options.text: Refer for a lumbar epidural corticosteroid injection before changing prescribing
options.rationale: Epidural corticosteroid has a limited role in radicular pain with clear nerve root compression and provides short lived benefit at best, and he has no radicular signs. Deferring the prescribing problem behind a procedural referral leaves multiple sourcing and escalating use running for months. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Analgesic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Analgesic

explanation.summary: Long term opioid therapy for chronic non cancer pain produces modest analgesic benefit that attenuates over time, while harms accumulate with dose, and Australian guidance recommends keeping doses below 50 mg oral morphine equivalent daily and reviewing carefully above that. Real time prescription monitoring is now operating across Australian jurisdictions and reveals multiple prescriber use that was previously invisible, which is best raised openly with the patient rather than treated as an accusation. Early requests, multiple sources, declining function and loss of analgesic effect together indicate that the treatment is failing and may signal an emerging opioid use disorder, which is assessed on the criteria of impaired control, social impairment, risky use and pharmacological features. Tapering is the intervention, undertaken slowly at around ten per cent of the dose every two to four weeks with faster reduction early and slower reduction at low doses, alongside active non opioid pain management and treatment of sleep and mood. Where a taper repeatedly fails or a use disorder is diagnosed, transfer to buprenorphine or methadone through an opioid treatment programme is the appropriate step rather than continued escalation.
key_points: Benefit attenuates over time while dose related harm continues to accumulate
Real time prescription monitoring reveals multiple sourcing and should be raised openly
Abrupt cessation increases overdose death and suicide and drives illicit sourcing
Taper at about ten per cent every two to four weeks with non opioid pain management
A failed taper or a diagnosed use disorder warrants transfer to buprenorphine
explanation.pearls: Prescribe take home naloxone at the same consultation: anyone on more than 50 mg oral morphine equivalent daily is in the higher risk group for overdose, and it is available without prescription in Australian pharmacies under the take home naloxone programme, so the barrier is the conversation rather than the cost.

sources.label: RACGP: Prescribing drugs of dependence in general practice

subtopic_detail: Dense anterograde amnesia with confabulation and preserved attention three weeks into abstinence after repeated withdrawals
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to review a 58 year old man on the medical ward three weeks after admission for his third episode of alcohol withdrawal this year. The team is planning to discharge him tomorrow to live alone in his flat.

Nursing staff report that he tells them warmly about going fishing with his brother yesterday and about the hospital cafe he visited this morning, neither of which happened, and he has not left the ward. He greets you as though you have not met, although you assessed him this morning. He converses fluently, names objects without difficulty, follows a three stage command and can subtract serial sevens accurately. He was given three days of oral thiamine tablets at admission.

data_table.Examination: Alert with sustained attention through a twenty minute interview, months of the year backwards performed accurately, recall of three words at five minutes zero out of three, broad based unsteady gait, no nystagmus and full eye movements, no tremor or agitation
data_table.Investigations: Montreal Cognitive Assessment 19 out of 30 with points lost predominantly on delayed recall, full blood count shows macrocytosis, liver function shows a raised gamma glutamyl transferase, urea creatinine and electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and folate within normal limits, computed tomography of the brain shows mild generalised atrophy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give high dose parenteral thiamine and defer the decision about where he lives
options.rationale: Dense anterograde amnesia with confabulation and preserved attention, fluency and executive function is the amnestic syndrome that follows inadequately treated thiamine deficiency, and three days of oral tablets is far short of what is required because oral absorption is saturable and impaired in people who drink heavily. Cognition continues to recover over three to twelve months with abstinence and adequate replacement, so placement, capacity and prognosis decisions made this week will be based on a floor he has not yet reached. (Source: NHMRC: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems)
source_refs: NHMRC: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems

options.text: Commence donepezil for probable Alzheimer disease and arrange clinic follow up
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibition is appropriate for Alzheimer disease, which presents with gradually progressive memory loss accompanied by word finding difficulty, visuospatial decline and functional deterioration over years. His deficit appeared abruptly in the context of repeated withdrawals, spares language and executive function, and has a treatable nutritional cause. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and management of cognitive impairment)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of cognitive impairment

options.text: Discharge him tomorrow as planned with community alcohol and drug follow up
options.rationale: Community follow up is an essential part of his care and should certainly be arranged. Discharging a man who cannot form new memories to live alone means he cannot reliably take medication, keep appointments, manage a stove or recall safety advice, and the amnesia itself will prevent him reporting that he is struggling. (Source: NHMRC: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems)
source_refs: NHMRC: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems

options.text: Arrange a capacity assessment today and apply for a guardianship order for him
options.rationale: A guardianship application may ultimately be needed if the impairment proves permanent and he cannot make accommodation decisions. Capacity is assessed at the point a decision must be made and can improve substantially over months here, so applying now risks imposing a durable legal order on the basis of a recoverable state. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and management of cognitive impairment)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of cognitive impairment

options.text: Commence an antipsychotic to address the false accounts he is giving to staff
options.rationale: Antipsychotic treatment targets delusions, which are fixed beliefs held with conviction and defended against evidence. Confabulation is the unintentional filling of a memory gap with plausible material, is not defended when challenged and varies from telling to telling, so it does not respond to dopamine blockade. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

explanation.summary: Wernicke encephalopathy results from thiamine deficiency and classically presents with confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia, although the full triad appears in only a minority and many cases are recognised only at autopsy. Untreated or inadequately treated episodes progress to Korsakoff syndrome, a chronic amnestic state characterised by dense anterograde amnesia, variable retrograde amnesia and confabulation, with attention, language and executive function relatively preserved. The dissociation between severely impaired delayed recall and intact attention is the key bedside finding, and it is what separates this from delirium, where attention is disturbed, and from Alzheimer disease, where other cognitive domains decline alongside memory. Australian guidance is to give parenteral thiamine to anyone with hazardous alcohol use who is admitted, because oral absorption is saturable and reduced by alcohol, and to give it before any glucose containing fluid, since a carbohydrate load consumes remaining thiamine and can precipitate the encephalopathy. Recovery in Korsakoff syndrome occurs in roughly a quarter and improves in many more over three to twelve months of abstinence and replacement, so definitive decisions about accommodation, capacity and prognosis are deferred until that trajectory is clear.
key_points: The classic triad is present in a minority and the diagnosis is frequently missed
Dense amnesia with preserved attention and language is the bedside signature
Confabulation is a memory gap filled in, not a delusion, and is not treated with antipsychotics
Oral thiamine absorption is saturable and inadequate in people who drink heavily
Cognition improves over three to twelve months, so placement decisions are deferred
explanation.pearls: Give parenteral thiamine before any glucose containing fluid in anyone with hazardous alcohol use: a carbohydrate load consumes the last of the remaining thiamine as a cofactor and can convert a subclinical deficiency into an irreversible amnestic syndrome within hours.

sources.label: NHMRC: Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems
RANZCP: Assessment and management of cognitive impairment

subtopic_detail: Nocturnal eating with complete amnesia for the episodes months after starting a non benzodiazepine hypnotic
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 42 year old woman who has taken zolpidem nightly for four months for insomnia that began during a stressful period at work.

Her partner tells you that she gets up an hour or two after falling asleep, goes to the kitchen and eats large quantities of whatever is there, including frozen bread and uncooked pasta, and does not answer when he speaks to her. She has no memory of any of it and has twice found the kitchen in disarray and been upset and frightened by it. She has sent two incoherent text messages overnight that she cannot recall writing. She does not eat in this way during the day, has no concerns about her weight or body shape, sleepwalked at no point in childhood, and drinks no alcohol.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 27 kg/m2 having risen from 24 kg/m2 over four months, normal affect with no low mood or anhedonia, no psychomotor change, neurological examination within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea creatinine and electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function and fasting glucose all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Halve the zolpidem dose and continue it alongside a consistent bedtime routine
options.rationale: Complex sleep behaviours are more frequent at higher doses, which makes dose reduction an intuitive response, and lower doses are recommended for women because of slower clearance. The reaction occurs at the lowest available dose as well, so continuing the drug at any dose leaves her at risk of an episode involving cooking, driving or leaving the house. (Source: TGA: Zolpidem safety advisory)
source_refs: TGA: Zolpidem safety advisory

options.text: Refer for eating disorder assessment and commence fluoxetine for binge eating
options.rationale: Binge eating disorder involves recurrent consumption of large amounts of food with loss of control, distress, and preoccupation with weight and shape, and responds to psychological therapy and fluoxetine. It occurs in wakefulness with full awareness and recall, whereas she is unresponsive during the episodes, has no memory of them and eats substances no one would choose while awake. (Source: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Arrange overnight polysomnography before making any change to her medication
options.rationale: A sleep study is used when nocturnal seizures are suspected or when the history is genuinely ambiguous, and it may be needed later if behaviours continue after the drug is withdrawn. The history here is characteristic and a study takes weeks to arrange, during which she remains exposed to a recognised and reversible cause. (Source: TGA: Zolpidem safety advisory)
source_refs: TGA: Zolpidem safety advisory

options.text: Switch to temazepam at an equivalent dose to maintain her sleep through the night
options.rationale: Temazepam acts on the same gamma aminobutyric acid receptor complex and also causes parasomnias, amnesia and next day impairment, so moving within the sedative hypnotic class does not remove the mechanism. Australian guidance limits all hypnotics in this class to short intermittent courses rather than nightly use for months. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Hypnotics and sedatives)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Hypnotics and sedatives

options.text: Cease the zolpidem and treat the insomnia with cognitive behavioural therapy
options.rationale: Eating, texting, walking or driving while not fully awake with no recollection afterwards is a complex sleep behaviour, a recognised adverse effect of this drug class that carries a regulatory warning in Australia, and the drug is stopped rather than reduced because episodes have occurred at all doses. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is the first line treatment for chronic insomnia in any case, outperforms hypnotics beyond the first few weeks and carries none of this risk. (Source: TGA: Zolpidem safety advisory)
source_refs: TGA: Zolpidem safety advisory

explanation.summary: Zolpidem acts selectively at the alpha 1 subunit of the gamma aminobutyric acid type A receptor and can produce complex sleep behaviours in which a person carries out purposeful activity while not fully awake and has no memory of it afterwards. Reported behaviours include eating, cooking, making phone calls, having sex, leaving the house and driving, and Australian regulatory advice carries a specific warning about these events, including serious injuries and deaths. Risk rises with higher doses, with concurrent alcohol or other central nervous system depressants, and in women, who clear the drug more slowly. Because episodes occur at the lowest available dose, the response to any such event is permanent discontinuation rather than dose reduction, and switching to a benzodiazepine does not solve the problem since the mechanism is shared. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, covering stimulus control, sleep restriction, cognitive work and sleep hygiene, is the first line treatment for chronic insomnia in Australian guidance and maintains benefit after treatment ends, whereas hypnotics lose effect and are recommended only for short intermittent use.
key_points: Purposeful activity with no recall afterwards defines a complex sleep behaviour
Australian regulatory advice specifically warns about these events with this drug
Episodes occur at the lowest dose, so the drug is ceased rather than reduced
Benzodiazepines share the mechanism, so switching within the class does not help
Cognitive behavioural therapy is first line for chronic insomnia and outlasts hypnotics
explanation.pearls: Ask the bed partner rather than the patient when a hypnotic is being reviewed: the defining feature of these episodes is that the person has no memory of them, so a patient taking zolpidem will truthfully report no adverse effects while their partner has been watching them cook at three in the morning for months.

subtopic_detail: Seizure with profound hyponatraemia and maximally dilute urine in a man observed drinking continuously
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar called to the emergency department where a 38 year old man with schizophrenia, treated with olanzapine for six years, has had a generalised tonic clonic seizure lasting ninety seconds. He is now post ictal and drowsy but protecting his airway.

The nursing home staff who brought him in say he drinks constantly from taps and the bathroom shower, carries a two litre bottle everywhere, and that he looks visibly puffier in the evenings than in the mornings. He has had no vomiting, no diarrhoea and no recent change to his medication. He has not been started on any new drug and takes no diuretic.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 per minute, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy and rousable with no focal neurology, moist mucous membranes, jugular venous pressure not elevated, no peripheral oedema, weight 4.1 kg above his documented morning weight
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 112 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), serum osmolality 238 mOsm/kg (275-295), urine osmolality 78 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 12 mmol/L, thyroid function and morning cortisol within normal limits, computed tomography of the brain shows no acute abnormality

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Restrict all oral fluid with one to one observation and recheck the sodium
options.rationale: Strict fluid restriction with supervision is the definitive treatment for excessive water intake and will be needed as soon as he is stable, and the sodium then rises on its own as the free water is excreted. It acts far too slowly for a man who has already seized, where the cerebral oedema requires immediate reversal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Give a bolus of hypertonic saline and recheck the sodium within the hour
options.rationale: A seizure marks severe symptomatic hyponatraemia with cerebral oedema, and the treatment in that situation is a bolus of 3 per cent sodium chloride to raise the sodium by about 4 to 6 mmol/L quickly, irrespective of the underlying cause. The correction is then capped at no more than 8 to 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours, which matters especially here because a water loading picture corrects rapidly by itself once drinking stops. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Commence an infusion of isotonic saline at 125 mL per hour and monitor closely
options.rationale: Isotonic saline is the right fluid for hypovolaemic hyponatraemia, where volume repletion switches off antidiuretic hormone. With maximally dilute urine at 78 mOsm/kg the kidney is already excreting free water at full capacity, so isotonic fluid raises the sodium far too slowly for a seizing patient and can worsen it once the salt is excreted and the water retained. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Commence oral tolvaptan to promote free water clearance by the kidneys
options.rationale: Vasopressin receptor antagonists are used in the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, where the urine is inappropriately concentrated because antidiuretic hormone is being secreted. A urine osmolality of 78 mOsm/kg shows antidiuretic hormone is already fully suppressed, leaving no receptor activity for the drug to block. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Cease the olanzapine, since antipsychotic treatment is the likely precipitant
options.rationale: Antipsychotics and antidepressants can cause hyponatraemia through inappropriate antidiuresis, which would show a concentrated urine and typically appears within weeks of starting or changing the drug. He has taken the same agent for six years and his urine is maximally dilute, and stopping it abruptly risks psychotic relapse for no benefit. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antipsychotics)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antipsychotics

explanation.summary: Primary polydipsia occurs in up to a fifth of people with long standing schizophrenia and produces hyponatraemia when water intake exceeds the kidney's maximal excretion capacity of roughly 800 to 1000 mL per hour. The biochemical signature is a low serum osmolality with a maximally dilute urine below about 100 mOsm/kg, which separates it definitively from the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, where the urine is inappropriately concentrated, and from hypovolaemia, where urine sodium is low but urine osmolality is high. Diurnal weight gain of several kilograms across the day is a practical bedside marker used in inpatient units to detect water loading before it becomes dangerous. Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizures or coma is treated with hypertonic saline regardless of cause, because cerebral oedema is the immediate threat, and the total correction is then limited to 8 to 10 mmol/L over 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination. That limit demands particular care in water intoxication, since sodium can rise spontaneously by more than 10 mmol/L in a few hours once drinking stops and the kidney excretes the retained water.
key_points: Urine osmolality below 100 mOsm/kg indicates water intake exceeding excretion capacity
Inappropriate antidiuresis instead produces inappropriately concentrated urine
A seizure means hypertonic saline regardless of the underlying cause
Correction is limited to 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination
Diurnal weight gain is a practical bedside marker of water loading
explanation.pearls: Watch for overcorrection rather than undercorrection once the drinking stops: in water intoxication the kidney excretes the retained free water at up to a litre an hour, sodium can climb past the 10 mmol/L daily limit without any further treatment, and desmopressin is then given deliberately to hold the rise and prevent osmotic demyelination.

sources.label: RANZCP: Physical health of people with severe mental illness

subtopic_detail: Large volume dilute urine on long term lithium with a therapeutic level and no response to desmopressin
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 46 year old woman who has taken lithium for twelve years for bipolar affective disorder, with no episode of mania or depression in the past nine years. She now passes very large volumes of pale urine, gets up four times a night, and drinks constantly to keep up.

She has had no tremor, no vomiting, no diarrhoea and no unsteadiness, and has not started any new medication. She is frightened of becoming unwell again and says the last manic episode cost her her job and nearly her marriage.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 15 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Alert with no tremor, no ataxia, no hyperreflexia and no myoclonus, mucous membranes moist, no goitre, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Serum lithium 0.72 mmol/L (0.60-0.80), sodium 147 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine 84 micromol/L with estimated glomerular filtration rate above 60 mL/min/1.73m2, calcium and thyroid function within normal limits, 24 hour urine volume 5.2 litres, urine osmolality 105 mOsm/kg and unchanged after desmopressin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop lithium today and commence a thiazide diuretic to control the urine output
options.rationale: Thiazides paradoxically reduce urine volume in this condition by inducing mild volume contraction, and they are used as treatment, but they also reduce lithium clearance and raise the serum level into the toxic range if lithium is continued. Stopping lithium abruptly after twelve years of stability carries a high risk of rebound mania, so neither half of this option is safe as written. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Lithium)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Lithium

options.text: Give regular intranasal desmopressin to bring the urine output under control
options.rationale: Desmopressin replaces antidiuretic hormone and works when the deficiency is central, in the pituitary. The urine osmolality here did not change after desmopressin, which localises the defect to the collecting duct where the hormone is present but the receptor response is impaired. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Restrict her fluid intake to two litres daily and repeat the sodium in one week
options.rationale: Fluid restriction is the correct approach when polyuria is driven by excessive drinking, where the kidney is normal and restriction simply removes the load. Here the kidney cannot concentrate urine, so restricting intake while obligatory losses continue at over five litres a day would produce dangerous hypernatraemia, and her sodium is already 147 mmol/L. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Add amiloride and review whether lithium remains the best long term treatment
options.rationale: Lithium enters the principal cells of the collecting duct through the epithelial sodium channel and desensitises the vasopressin receptor, so blocking that channel with amiloride reduces lithium entry and improves concentrating ability while allowing lithium to continue. The parallel decision about whether to keep lithium is a genuine trade off, since nine years of stability on a drug with unmatched antisuicidal evidence has to be weighed against a renal effect that becomes irreversible with prolonged exposure. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Lithium)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Lithium

options.text: Increase the lithium dose to improve symptom control and recheck the level
options.rationale: Dose escalation would be considered if she were having breakthrough affective symptoms on a subtherapeutic level, and her level sits at 0.72 mmol/L with nine years of euthymia. Raising the dose worsens the tubular injury that is generating the polyuria in the first place. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Lithium)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Lithium

explanation.summary: Lithium induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus affects up to around a fifth of people on long term treatment and occurs at therapeutic levels, so a normal lithium concentration does not exclude it. Lithium enters principal cells of the collecting duct through the epithelial sodium channel and downregulates aquaporin 2 expression, leaving the tubule unable to respond to circulating vasopressin. The diagnosis is confirmed by polyuria with a dilute urine that fails to concentrate after desmopressin, which separates it from central diabetes insipidus, and by the absence of the diurnal weight gain and suppressed sodium seen in primary polydipsia. Amiloride blocks the channel through which lithium enters and is the specific treatment, with thiazides an alternative that requires lithium dose reduction and close level monitoring because they reduce lithium clearance. Free access to water is essential, since these patients decompensate rapidly into hypernatraemia when intake is interrupted by surgery, illness or a confusional state. Early changes may reverse on stopping lithium, but prolonged exposure produces irreversible tubulointerstitial change, and the decision to continue balances that risk against the drug's efficacy and its evidence for reducing suicide.
key_points: It occurs at therapeutic lithium levels, so a normal level does not exclude it
Failure to concentrate urine after desmopressin localises the defect to the tubule
Amiloride blocks lithium entry into principal cells and is the specific treatment
Thiazides work but reduce lithium clearance and demand dose reduction
Free water access is essential and interruption causes rapid hypernatraemia
explanation.pearls: Flag the polyuria in her perioperative and sick day planning as well as treating it: a fasting patient with obligatory losses above five litres a day becomes profoundly hypernatraemic within hours of being made nil by mouth, which is how lithium related concentrating defects most often cause harm.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood disorders clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Orofacial choreoathetoid movements emerging on long term depot treatment and worsening after a dose reduction
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 61 year old man with schizophrenia who has received a haloperidol depot injection for nine years. His sister says his mouth has been moving on its own for about two years and that it has become much more noticeable since his dose was reduced three months ago.

He is not troubled by the movements himself but they stop when he is asked to perform a task with his hands, and his sister reports he is now reluctant to eat in public. His psychotic symptoms have remained well controlled and he has had no relapse in five years.

data_table.Examination: Repetitive lip smacking, tongue protrusion and chewing movements with choreoathetoid movements of the fingers, present at rest and suppressed briefly on distraction, no cogwheel rigidity, no resting tremor, no bradykinesia, gait normal with preserved arm swing
data_table.Investigations: Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale score 14, full blood count, urea creatinine and electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function and copper studies all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase the depot dose back to the previous level to settle the movements
options.rationale: Raising the dose does mask the movements for weeks to months, because stronger receptor blockade suppresses the expression of the underlying supersensitivity, and the worsening after his reduction is the same phenomenon in reverse. It deepens the underlying process and makes the movements harder to treat later, which is why it is the classic anti-pattern in this condition. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Add benztropine regularly to treat the abnormal involuntary movements
options.rationale: Anticholinergic agents relieve acute dystonia and drug induced parkinsonism, where the problem is relative cholinergic excess, and they are effective and appropriate there. In tardive dyskinesia they worsen the movements and impair cognition, which is the opposite relationship and a common prescribing error. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Switch to an antipsychotic with a substantially lower risk of movement effects
options.rationale: Persistent orofacial choreoathetosis that emerged on long term treatment with a high potency first generation agent and worsened on dose reduction is tardive dyskinesia, and the first management step is to move to an agent with lower dopamine receptor affinity, with clozapine having the best evidence and quetiapine a reasonable alternative. The switch is made gradually because abrupt withdrawal transiently worsens the movements, and his five years of stability means psychotic relapse risk must be managed through the change. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

options.text: Add propranolol to reduce the frequency of the abnormal movements
options.rationale: Beta blockade is used for akathisia, the subjective inner restlessness with an urge to move that typically appears within weeks of starting or increasing an antipsychotic. His movements are involuntary and he is not distressed by an urge to move, which places them in a different category. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic

options.text: Cease all antipsychotic treatment immediately and observe over three months
options.rationale: Complete withdrawal is occasionally appropriate where the original indication is doubtful, and the movements may remit in a minority of people over months to years. Abrupt cessation transiently worsens dyskinesia and, in a man with schizophrenia stable for five years, carries a high risk of relapse. (Source: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

explanation.summary: Tardive dyskinesia develops in around a quarter of people on long term first generation antipsychotics and at lower but still significant rates with second generation agents, with older age, female sex, diabetes, cumulative exposure and earlier acute movement effects among the risk factors. It is thought to reflect dopamine receptor supersensitivity, which explains the two characteristic behaviours that confirm the diagnosis at the bedside: the movements worsen when the dose is reduced and are masked when it is increased. The picture is orofacial choreoathetosis with lip smacking, chewing and tongue movements, often with limb and trunk involvement, and it is distinguished from drug induced parkinsonism by the absence of rigidity, bradykinesia and resting tremor, and from akathisia by the absence of subjective restlessness. Management begins with reviewing the need for antipsychotic treatment, then switching to an agent with lower liability, and clozapine has the strongest evidence for improvement. Vesicular monoamine transporter 2 inhibitors such as valbenazine and deutetrabenazine are effective and registered overseas but are not subsidised in Australia, so tetrabenazine is the agent generally used, and anticholinergics must be stopped because they aggravate the movements.
key_points: Worsening on dose reduction and masking on dose increase confirm the mechanism
Absence of rigidity and bradykinesia separates it from drug induced parkinsonism
Anticholinergics aggravate tardive dyskinesia and should be withdrawn
Switching to a lower liability agent is the first step, with clozapine best supported
Tetrabenazine is the pharmacological option generally available in Australia
explanation.pearls: Rate the movements on the Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale at every change of antipsychotic rather than relying on impression: a transient worsening in the weeks after switching is expected as receptor blockade falls, and without a documented baseline score that predictable rebound gets misread as failure of the switch.

sources.label: RANZCP: Schizophrenia and related disorders clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Delusional misidentification of a spouse with fluctuating attention, dream enactment and later emerging parkinsonism
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar asked by a general practitioner to advise on a 76 year old man whose wife of fifty years reports that for eight months he has insisted she is an impostor who has replaced his real wife. He becomes frightened and occasionally pushes past her to look for the real one, and she is now sleeping at her daughter's house two nights a week.

He also describes seeing small children and a cat in the hallway, which he accepts are not always there. His wife says he has some days when he is sharp and other days when he stares into space for long periods and cannot follow a conversation. For three years before any of this he has shouted and thrashed in his sleep, once striking her, and he has always remembered a vivid dream afterwards. In the past two months he has become slower to start walking and has fallen twice. The general practitioner has written asking you to endorse starting risperidone.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72 per minute, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg lying and 116/70 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Mild symmetrical bradykinesia with reduced arm swing and a low amplitude rest tremor of the left hand, no cogwheeling at the neck, fluctuating attention through the interview with two episodes of staring, no focal weakness, gait slow with reduced stride length
data_table.Investigations: Mini Mental State Examination 24 out of 30 with marked visuospatial impairment on pentagon copying, full blood count, urea creatinine and electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and midstream urine all within normal limits, computed tomography of the brain shows generalised atrophy without infarction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence rivastigmine and advise against antipsychotic treatment at this stage
options.rationale: Dream enactment predating cognitive change, fluctuating attention, formed visual hallucinations, visuospatial impairment out of proportion to memory and parkinsonism emerging after the cognitive symptoms together indicate Lewy body disease, in which up to half of patients have a severe sensitivity reaction to dopamine blockade with rigidity, confusion, autonomic instability and a two to threefold increase in mortality. Cholinesterase inhibition is the treatment with the best evidence for the hallucinations and delusions in this condition and improves attention as well. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia

options.text: Commence low dose risperidone as requested and monitor for movement effects
options.rationale: Risperidone is the only antipsychotic registered in Australia for behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia and would be defensible in Alzheimer disease with persisting aggression after non pharmacological measures. It is a potent dopamine blocker, and in Lewy body disease that is precisely the exposure that precipitates the severe sensitivity reaction, so monitoring does not make it safe. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia

options.text: Commence low dose quetiapine, which has the least dopamine blocking activity
options.rationale: Quetiapine has the lowest striatal dopamine receptor occupancy of the available agents and is the one usually chosen when antipsychotic treatment is genuinely unavoidable in this condition. Its randomised evidence for efficacy in Lewy body disease is weak, severe sensitivity reactions have still been reported with it, and it adds orthostatic hypotension and sedation to a man who already has a postural blood pressure drop and two recent falls. (Source: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Assessment and management of people with behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia

options.text: Commence levodopa to treat the parkinsonism and reassess the psychotic symptoms
options.rationale: Levodopa is used cautiously for disabling motor symptoms in this condition, starting low and increasing slowly, once the neuropsychiatric picture is stable. Introducing dopaminergic treatment while florid hallucinations and a persecutory misidentification are present predictably aggravates them, and the motor symptoms here are mild. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology

options.text: Commence a benzodiazepine at night and review the situation again in four weeks
options.rationale: Clonazepam or melatonin is used for the dream enactment component of this illness and would address one symptom, and melatonin is generally preferred given its better safety profile. Benzodiazepines worsen confusion and falls in a man with fluctuating attention and postural hypotension, and they do nothing for the delusion that is driving his wife out of the house. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology

explanation.summary: Dementia with Lewy bodies accounts for a substantial share of dementia in Australia yet is frequently misdiagnosed as Alzheimer disease or late onset psychosis, and the consequences of that error are serious because standard treatment for either can be dangerous. The core clinical features are fluctuating cognition with pronounced variation in attention and alertness, recurrent well formed visual hallucinations, rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder, and spontaneous parkinsonism, with the timing rule that cognitive symptoms precede or accompany motor symptoms within a year. Delusional misidentification, in which a familiar person is believed to have been replaced by an impostor, is far more characteristic of Lewy body disease than of Alzheimer disease and is a common trigger for an antipsychotic request. Severe neuroleptic sensitivity occurs in up to half of these patients and can be fatal, so management starts with review of contributing medications, non pharmacological strategies and carer safety planning, then a cholinesterase inhibitor, for which the evidence in this condition is stronger than in any other dementia. Where an antipsychotic is unavoidable, quetiapine or clozapine at the lowest effective dose is used with full documentation of the risk, and the dream enactment is treated separately with melatonin or low dose clonazepam.
key_points: Dream enactment often precedes cognitive change by years and is a strong pointer
Fluctuating attention with formed visual hallucinations distinguishes it from Alzheimer disease
Impostor delusions about a spouse are characteristic of Lewy body disease
Severe neuroleptic sensitivity occurs in up to half and carries excess mortality
Cholinesterase inhibitors have their strongest dementia evidence in this condition
explanation.pearls: Ask the partner whether he has acted out dreams during sleep, and how long that has been happening: dream enactment commonly predates the cognitive decline by five to ten years, it is the single most specific pointer to Lewy body disease, and eliciting it is what stops a request for risperidone becoming a fatal sensitivity reaction.
